title: IPO Underpricing and On-Chain Issuance
subtitle: How the IPO process systematically underprices new listings, what has changed in regulation, technology, and capital, and where blockchain-based auctions fit.
body_html:
IPOs are a lossy fundraising method. At least for now. Roughly $13B was left on the table across 90 operating-company IPOs last year. The average one-day return? 29.3%1. This pattern is persistent across times and geographies, and benefits underwriters and those provided allocations, at the expense of the offering company and its pre-IPO shareholders.

Why Are Things This Way?

  1. IPOs are a repeated game between investment banks and institutional investors, and a single-period game between the company going public and its underwriters. Deals are systematically oversubscribed and underpriced, providing institutional investors primary market entries well below the clearing price.2 This helps investment banks maintain the relationships needed for future offerings. Listing companies, contrastingly, tend to go public once.

  2. Underwriting banks are also subject to an asymmetric loss function around day-one price movement. If the stock of a newly issued company performs well in the hours following its IPO, the investment bank loses nothing. If the stock trends down, the underwriter risks being stuck with unsold shares, faces lawsuits, and hurts the institutional clients who bought the deal3. Through this lens, the behavioral patterns of underwriters are interpretable: banks don't want underperforming listings, sub-clearing prices heavily reduce the likelihood of underperformance, and the banks have discretion over primary market prices. So prices tend to be low. Tellingly, when an already-public company raises more equity, through the same banks and the same process, the discount is only ~2–3%.4

Why Is This Undesirable?

Perhaps this is self-evident, but to spell it out: IPO inefficiencies act as a capital transfer from companies and pre-IPO shareholders to risk-insulated middlemen and privileged capital allocators offered favorable entry points. That’s a bad equilibrium. Public offerings are meant for capitalization and insider exit liquidity at market-clearing levels, not contrived, systematically stunted valuations.

What’s Changed?

While the above is a well-worn line of criticism, a combination of regulatory, technological, and capital accessibility barriers has historically offered an excuse for accepting the status quo. Today’s conditions may challenge that.

Regulation: Before 2020, a company could not raise new capital in an exchange listing without an underwriter. Then the SEC approved the New York Stock Exchange’s proposal to allow private companies to conduct an IPO as part of a direct listing. The Nasdaq equivalent came in 20215. This provided companies a means of side-stepping the previously unavoidable web of misaligned incentives defining the relationships between underwriters, issuing companies, and institutional investors. The relief was narrow, as it applies only to auctions run by the exchanges themselves. But it established that a company can raise primary capital without banks underwriting the deal or deciding who gets shares, provided regulators accept the venue running the auction.

Technology: The lack of a mandate for an underwriter loosened one constraint, but is insufficient on its own. Without underwriters, an issuing company must find a means of securing committed capital at scale. Enter blockchains: on-chain, bids can be pre-funded and held in escrow, so an issuer knows its proceeds before the auction clears.

Capital Accessibility: That IPOs may no longer need underwriting matters only insofar as there is capital positioned to take advantage of the opportunity. The first suggestion that this may be so is from the initial coin offering (“ICO”) movement in the mid-2010s. ICOs, as unscrupulous as they were, showed that financial resources could be directed towards a common purpose by a large, decentralized set of actors. Across 2017 and 2018, ICOs raised ~$20B. That’s half of what the U.S. IPO market raised last year.

Since then, the scale of on-chain value has increased massively, and changed in composition. Tokenized real-world assets, which barely existed during the ICO boom, are worth ~$38B today. Stablecoins, the cash any on-chain auction would settle in, add another ~$300B.

While a capitalization event on the scale of the SpaceX IPO ($75B raised)6 is likely out of reach for the time being, the average IPO is on the order of hundreds of millions of dollars. For these smaller, more typical offerings, raising capital on-chain is a plausible proposition. Picture a sealed-bid auction where every bid is pre-funded in stablecoins, institutions and individuals bid side by side, and every winner pays the same market-clearing price.7 No banker decides who gets shares or at what price, and the issuer knows its proceeds the moment the auction clears.

The open question is whether regulators would accept a blockchain as the venue, the way they accepted the exchanges in 2020.8

None of this means that the way IPOs are done today will be replaced tomorrow. The point here is that, for the first time, the traditional reasons why IPOs have to work this way may not hold.

1

The median was 13.7% because a handful of huge pops pull the average up.

2

Reuter (Journal of Finance, 2006) finds funds that pay underwriters more in commissions receive larger IPO allocations. In 2002, Credit Suisse First Boston paid $100M to settle SEC and NASD charges that it handed out hot IPO shares in exchange for inflated commissions.

3

Banks do have some downside protection. Underwriters typically sell 15% more shares than the base deal and hold an option to buy them from the issuer at the offer price (the "greenshoe"). If the stock falls, they buy those shares back in the market instead, below the offer price, at a profit.

4

Banker incentives aren't the only explanation. Others include compensating institutions for revealing price information during the roadshow (Benveniste and Spindt, 1989) and protecting uninformed bidders from overpaying (Rock, 1986).

5

Companies still file a price range with the SEC, and the auction must clear within a band around it (on Nasdaq, 20% below to 80% above). A named underwriter is still required for securities-law liability. Most importantly, no primary direct listings appear to have been used.

6

It also closed its first day up 19%, roughly $14B left on the table, more than all 90 IPOs of 2025 combined.

7

Auctions aren't new. Google used one for its 2004 IPO and still rose about 18% on day one. Putting the auction on-chain changes who can bid and how bids settle.

8

The SEC has started down this road. Its September 2026 Innovation Exemption lets tokenized versions of listed stocks trade on approved on-chain venues. It covers trading, not issuance.
